title: Plug-&-Play Traffic Light
pitch: The easiest first project: a traffic-light module with built-in resistors, just 4 wires and you're running.

guide.about: This module already has a resistor for each LED, so there's nothing to calculate. Plug in 4 wires, upload, done. Perfect for your very first upload.
parts: the little board with red, yellow and green LEDs
steps: Connect the module's R, Y and G pins to board pins 4, 3 and 2.
Connect the module's GND to a GND pin.
Upload the code.
Watch it cycle, then try changing the times in the code.
guide.test: Green 5 s → yellow 2 s → red 5 s → red+yellow 1 s → green again.
next: Add a button for a pedestrian crossing (see Mini Traffic Light).
Build two and make a crossroads.

title: Shield Egg Timer
pitch: An LCD Keypad Shield becomes a kitchen timer with menus: set minutes and seconds with the buttons, no wiring at all.

guide.about: The shield's 5 buttons all share one analog pin: each button makes a different voltage. You'll learn to tell them apart by their analogRead() value.
wiring: Plugs on top of the board
through 220Ω, under the shield or on its spare holes; − to GND
steps: Press the shield onto the board carefully so all pins go in.
(Optional) Connect a passive buzzer to Pin 3 through 220Ω and GND.
Upload. Adjust the blue screw on the shield if the text is invisible.
UP/DOWN change the value, LEFT/RIGHT switch between minutes and seconds, SELECT starts or stops.
guide.test: Set 0:10 and press SELECT: it counts down and flashes TIME'S UP (with beeps if you added a buzzer). If buttons act strangely, the Serial Monitor (9600) shows their values: adjust the thresholds.
next: Add presets: soft egg, hard egg, tea.
Remember the last time in EEPROM.

title: Scrolling Name Sign
pitch: Your name (or any message) scrolls across a glowing 32x8 LED sign. Great for desks, doors and cosplay.

guide.about: The code has its own 5x7 pixel font. Each letter is 5 columns of bits, and the message slides one column at a time across four chained MAX7219 matrices.
wiring: the input end of the module
steps: Install the LedControl library.
Wire the module's input side (DIN end): VCC 5V, GND, DIN 12, CS 10, CLK 11.
Type your message into MESSAGE in the code (A–Z, 0–9 and basic symbols).
Upload.
4-in-1 modules come in different layouts. If the text is mirrored, upside down or jumbled, flip REVERSE_DEVICES, ROTATE or FLIP in the code one at a time until it reads correctly.
guide.test: The message scrolls smoothly from right to left and repeats.
safety: 32x8 LEDs can draw almost 1A at full brightness: keep INTENSITY low on USB power.
next: Show the time with a DS3231.
Change the message from your phone (see Wi-Fi Scrolling Sign).

title: RGB Emoji Matrix
pitch: Full-color pixel emoji on an 8x8 RGB LED panel: hearts, smileys, a slime, a ghost… press a button for the next one.

guide.about: Each picture is 64 numbers, one color index per pixel. You'll learn how 2D pictures become a 1D list of LEDs, and how to keep brightness safe for USB power.
steps: Install Adafruit NeoPixel.
Wire the matrix (DIN through 330Ω to Pin 6) and the button (Pin 2).
Upload. Brightness is capped at a safe level for USB.
If pictures look scrambled every other row, set SERPENTINE to true.
guide.test: A heart appears; each press shows the next emoji: smiley, slime, ghost, star, mushroom-free space invader-ish alien… original pixel art!
safety: 64 RGB LEDs at full white can draw ~3.8A. Keep BRIGHTNESS low on USB, or use a 5V 4A supply.
next: Animate them with two frames each.
Draw your own 8x8 art on graph paper.

title: 12V Shelf Light Dimmer
pitch: A smooth knob-controlled dimmer for a 12V white LED strip: perfect under a shelf or desk.

guide.about: The strip runs on 12V from a wall adapter; the board only controls the MOSFET's gate with PWM. LED strips are not motors, so no flyback diode is needed.
wiring: through 220Ω, plus 10kΩ from Gate to GND
steps: Build the MOSFET switch on the breadboard (label facing you: Gate, Drain, Source).
Connect the strip: + to the 12V terminal, − to the Drain.
Connect the Source to the breakout's GND AND to the board's GND.
Wire the potentiometer to A0, power the board from USB, upload.
Plug in the 12V adapter last and turn the knob.
guide.test: The strip fades in at power-up, then follows the knob smoothly from off to full brightness.
safety: Double-check that 12V never touches the board's pins. Only the MOSFET connects the two circuits (via GND).
Use wires thick enough for the strip's current (about 1A per metre).
next: Add a PIR so it switches on when you approach.
Use a light sensor for automatic night mode.

title: Smart Cooling Fan
pitch: A 12V PC fan that switches itself on when the room (or your gaming console's shelf) gets too warm.

guide.about: A thermostat with "hysteresis": on above 28°C, off below 26°C, so it doesn't flicker on and off. The 12V adapter powers the board through its jack, and the fan takes 12V from the VIN pin.
parts: plugs into the board's barrel jack
wiring: the board's VIN pin now carries ~12V
steps: Install DHT sensor library and Adafruit Unified Sensor.
Build the MOSFET switch and connect the fan between VIN and the Drain, with the diode across the fan (stripe to VIN).
Wire the DHT11 to 5V, GND and Pin 2.
Upload over USB, then unplug USB and plug the 12V adapter into the barrel jack.
Warm the sensor with your hand (or a hair dryer from a distance) to test.
guide.test: Above 28°C the fan spins up; below 26°C it stops. The Serial Monitor (with USB connected) shows temperature and fan state.
safety: Never touch VIN to other pins: it carries 12V when the adapter is plugged in.
Keep fingers out of the fan blades.
next: Show the temperature on a TM1637.
Change ON_C/OFF_C for your console or 3D printer enclosure.

title: Desk Drum Bot
pitch: A 12V solenoid taps out drum rhythms on your desk, a cup or a box. Robot percussion!

guide.about: A solenoid is an electromagnet that shoots a pin out. Short 30 ms pulses make clean taps without overheating it. Patterns are stored as strings like "x..x..x.".
steps: Build the MOSFET switch and wire the solenoid between +12V and the Drain.
Put the diode across the solenoid, stripe toward +12V. Don't skip this!
Connect all grounds together. Power the board from USB.
Upload, then plug in the 12V adapter.
Point the solenoid's plunger at something fun to hit and press the button.
guide.test: It plays a rhythm pattern, switching to a new one every 8 bars. Turn the knob for faster or slower tempo.
safety: Short pulses only: the code limits each hit to 30 ms. A solenoid held on gets very hot.
Keep fingers away from the plunger.
next: Add a second solenoid for a two-drum kit.
Trigger hits from a MIDI keyboard or your PC.

title: Precision Stepper Spinner
pitch: Drive a strong NEMA 17 stepper (the 3D-printer motor) with a speed knob and a direction button.

guide.about: The A4988 does the heavy lifting: each pulse on STEP moves the motor one step (200 per turn). You'll generate precise pulses with micros() and learn why the driver's current limit matters.
wiring: 100µF capacitor across VMOT and GND, close to the driver
one coil on 1A/1B, the other on 2A/2B (check the motor's datasheet)
a short jumper between the two pins
steps: Put the A4988 on the breadboard and connect RESET to SLEEP.
Wire VDD/GND to the board, VMOT/GND to the 12V breakout, with the 100µF capacitor (stripe to GND) right next to VMOT.

Set the current limit BEFORE connecting the motor: with 12V on, measure the voltage between the driver's small screw and GND, and adjust it as your board's datasheet describes (roughly Vref = motor current × 8 × sense resistor, aim for ~70% of the motor's rating).
Switch everything off, connect the motor's two coils, then wire STEP (3), DIR (4), the pot (A0) and the button (2).
Upload, then plug in the 12V adapter and turn the knob.
guide.test: The motor spins smoothly from 0 to about 120 RPM following the knob; the button reverses direction.
safety: Never connect or disconnect the motor while the driver is powered: it can destroy the A4988.
The driver and motor get hot: keep the heatsink on and don't touch them while running.
If you're not sure about the current-limit formula for your A4988 clone, start low: the motor just gets weaker, nothing breaks.
next: Add microstepping (MS1–MS3) for smoother motion.
Build a camera slider or a precise turntable.

title: Door Open Chime
pitch: A shop-style ding when the door opens, plus a reminder beep if it's left open. It also counts visitors.

guide.about: The MC-38 is a magnet and a reed switch. While the door is closed, the magnet holds the switch closed (the pin reads LOW). Opening the door breaks the circuit.
parts: screw or tape: magnet on the door, switch on the frame
steps: Mount the switch part on the door frame and the magnet part on the door, less than 1 cm apart when closed.
Run the two wires to Pin 2 and GND.
Wire the buzzer through 220Ω to Pin 8.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
guide.test: Opening the door plays a ding-dong and prints the visitor count. Leave it open for 60 s and it beeps a reminder every 10 s.
next: Send a phone alert with an ESP32 instead.
Count visitors per day and show it on an LCD.

title: Bike Tamper Alarm
pitch: Arm it, walk away, and if someone shakes your bike (or your secret box), a loud siren goes off.

guide.about: The SW-420 notices vibration. To avoid false alarms, the code needs several shakes within 2 seconds before it sounds the siren, plus a 10-second exit delay after arming.
steps: Wire the sensor (DO → Pin 2), button (Pin 4) and buzzer (Pin 8).
Upload and open the Serial Monitor (9600). Tap the sensor and adjust its screw so taps register but sitting still doesn't.
Put everything in a small box with a power bank and attach it to your bike.
Press the button: the LED blinks for 10 s (walk away), then stays on: armed!
guide.test: Armed + several shakes = 15 s siren. Press the button any time to disarm.
next: Add a keypad code to disarm.
Add a GPS module to track the bike.

title: 4-Servo Robot Arm
pitch: Control a little robot arm (base, shoulder, elbow, claw) with two joysticks. Pick things up!

guide.about: The PCA9685 board generates servo signals for up to 16 servos over just 2 wires (I2C), and takes servo power from its own terminal, so the board never has to supply the current.
parts: or MG90S: base, shoulder, elbow, claw
wiring: base, shoulder, elbow, claw (brown wire = GND side)
steps: Install the Adafruit PWM Servo Driver Library.
Build the arm: a cardboard or printed arm kit, or stack the servos with their horns and some hot glue.
Wire the PCA9685 to 5V, GND, A4, A5. Connect the battery pack to its screw terminal (check + and −!).
Plug the servos into channels 0–3 (signal pin toward the top).
Wire both joysticks to A0–A3.
Upload. The arm moves to a middle pose. Tilt the sticks to move each joint.
guide.test: Holding a stick tilted keeps moving that joint; releasing stops it where it is. The claw opens and closes with joystick 2's Y axis.
safety: Servos get their power only from the battery pack on the PCA9685 terminal, never from the board.
If a servo buzzes at the end of its travel, reduce MIN/MAX in the code so it doesn't strain.
next: Add record & playback of movements.
Control it from your phone with an ESP32.

title: Uno R4 Matrix Mood Faces
pitch: The Uno R4 WiFi has a built-in red LED matrix. Make it show animated mood faces, with no extra parts.

guide.about: The R4 WiFi's 12x8 matrix is driven by the built-in Arduino_LED_Matrix library. Each face is a 12x8 grid of 1s and 0s.
steps: Install the "Arduino UNO R4 Boards" package in Boards Manager if you haven't.
Choose Tools → Board → Arduino UNO R4 WiFi.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 (Newline).
Type happy, sad, wow, love or sleep and press Enter.
guide.test: The matrix shows a face that blinks every few seconds, and changes when you type a mood.
next: Show Wi-Fi status with icons.
React to a sensor: sad when it's too hot.
